title: Upper Airway & Larynx Anatomy: Cartilages & Vocal Folds
description: Learn upper airway and larynx anatomy from the nasal conchae and three pharyngeal regions to the epiglottis, laryngeal cartilages, vocal folds, and airway.
h1: Upper Airway and Larynx Anatomy: Pharynx, Cartilages and Vocal Folds
blurb: Warming nasal conchae, the three-part pharynx, and the nine cartilages of the larynx that protect the lower airway during swallowing and vibrate vocal folds.
lead: At the crossroads of breathing and swallowing, the upper airway warms and filters inspired air while the cartilaginous larynx guards the lungs and generates the human voice. In this illustrated guide to upper airway and larynx anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including nasal cavity & conchae, paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx & adenoid, oropharynx—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: At the crossroads of breathing and swallowing, the upper airway warms and filters inspired air while the cartilaginous larynx guards the lungs and generates the human voice. Midsagittal cut from nasal conchae to tracheal rings — including the parts you cannot see from outside: sinuses, adenoid, vocal folds. Within the human body, the upper airway (Via aerea superior) is situated in nose to trachea, receives arterial perfusion via branches of external & internal carotid, and is innervated by vagus (IX/X for pharynx).

The nasal cavity & conchae (Cavum nasi) is three conchae turbo-charge the surface area. Physiologically, the nasal cavity & conchae warms, humidifies and filters inspired air. Structurally, the paranasal sinuses (Sinus paranasales) comprises frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, sphenoid air spaces. Physiologically, the paranasal sinuses governs lighten the skull; resonate voice; humidify. The nasopharynx & adenoid (Nasopharynx) is posterior nasal chamber with lymphoid adenoid. Physiologically, the nasopharynx & adenoid governs air passage; immune sampling in childhood. Anatomically, the oropharynx lies behind the mouth, tonsils at its sides. Physiologically, the oropharynx governs shared food–air corridor; speech resonance. The epiglottis is elastic leaf above the larynx. Physiologically, the epiglottis governs flips to cover the larynx during swallowing. Structurally, the larynx comprises thyroid + cricoid cartilages housing the folds. Physiologically, the larynx governs voice production and airway protection.

Clinically, regarding the nasal cavity & conchae, deviated septum + turbinate hypertrophy = blocked nose. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the paranasal sinuses, sinusitis pain follows the sinus walls — maxillary = cheekache. In clinical pathology involving the nasopharynx & adenoid, adenoid hypertrophy causes snoring and glue ear in kids. Medical evaluation of the oropharynx also notes that OSA collapse happens here during sleep.

questions.question: What is the path of air through the upper airway?
questions.answer: Air passes from the nose or mouth through the pharynx and larynx, then down the trachea toward the bronchi.

questions.question: What does the epiglottis do during swallowing?
questions.answer: The epiglottis is one structure involved in protecting the laryngeal entrance during swallowing; coordinated movement of the larynx and vocal folds also matters.

questions.question: What are the nasal cavity and nasal conchae?
questions.answer: The nasal cavity is divided by a septum and contains three conchae on each side that increase surface area and create airflow turbulence.

questions.question: Where are the nasopharynx and adenoid located?
questions.answer: The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate; the adenoid is in its roof and posterior wall.

questions.question: Where is the epiglottis located?
questions.answer: The epiglottis is an elastic-cartilage flap at the laryngeal inlet, behind the tongue base and attached to the thyroid cartilage by a ligament.
